pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Two goroutines each run `n++` 1000 times with no synchronization. What final values are possible, and what does `go test -race` say about it?
expected_points: n++ is load, add, store — three steps that can interleave
updates get lost, so the total can be anything up to 2000, and a racy program has no defined behavior at all
the race detector reports a read and a previous write at the same address, with the goroutines and source lines
adding a mutex around the increment (or using an atomic) fixes it

questions.prompt: You have a config store read on every request and rewritten once a minute. Mutex or RWMutex — and what's your reasoning? When would the answer flip?
expected_points: RWMutex: reads vastly outnumber writes, and RLock lets readers proceed in parallel
read-only methods take RLock, mutating methods take Lock; writing under RLock is a race
RWMutex costs more per operation, so with balanced read/write traffic or tiny critical sections a plain Mutex wins — default to Mutex and measure

questions.prompt: Two jobs: (a) lazily build one shared Config the first time any goroutine asks; (b) count requests served. Which sync tool fits each, and why not a plain `if cfg == nil` check or a plain `n++`?
expected_points: (a) sync.Once — Do runs the function exactly once and all callers wait for it and see its effects
`if cfg == nil` is check-then-act: two goroutines can both see nil and both load, plus the unsynchronized read races the write
(b) an atomic counter (atomic.Int64 Add/Load) — indivisible, no lock needed for a single word
plain n++ is three steps and loses updates

questions.prompt: You wrote channel pipelines last lesson and a mutex-guarded Counter here. How do you decide which tool a new problem gets?
expected_points: channels when data moves between goroutines — transferring ownership, distributing work, signaling
locks when state stays in one place and many goroutines access it — counters, caches, registries
atomics for single-word counters/flags; Once for one-time init; WaitGroup for waiting
either can be forced to do the other's job, but it costs code and clarity — match the tool to the shape

questions.prompt: A teammate writes `func (c Counter) Inc(name string)` on your mutex-holding Counter. Why is this a bug, and which tool catches it?
expected_points: a value receiver copies the struct, including the mutex — each call locks a fresh copy
the map inside is still shared, so the data is effectively unprotected
go vet's copylocks check reports 'passes lock by value'
sync types must not be copied after first use — use pointer receivers and pass pointers

questions.prompt: Hits and Misses are separate atomic.Int64s. A dashboard goroutine reads both to show a ratio. Any problem?
expected_points: each counter is individually race-free, but the pair is not updated as one step
the reader can observe a state between the two updates, so the ratio can be momentarily wrong
an invariant spanning multiple values needs a mutex around the compound update and read

questions.prompt: Your test suite passes with -race in CI for a month. Does that prove the code is race-free? How do you treat a report vs a clean run?
expected_points: no — the detector only sees races that occur in the interleavings actually executed
a clean run is evidence, not proof; coverage of concurrent paths matters
any report is a real bug to fix, never a flaky test to retry
